text: Archive started: the 2026 Quality Education Model report, revenue forecasts, budget documents, Gov. Kotek's record and the State School Fund history.
Profiles of the budget-writing legislators: Sen. Kate Lieber, Rep. Tawna Sanchez, Rep. Ricki Ruiz and Sen. Janeen Sollman.
A glossary of school funding abbreviations and terms.
Education Stability Fund balance and the rules for drawing on it.
The briefing (since replaced by What's being decided and topic pages), rewritten: what's being decided, how Measures 5 and 50 shaped school funding, the numbers, who stands where and what's next.
Gov. Kotek's Oct 13 letter to Portland Public Schools leaders, archived and quoted.
Online charter schools: how much State School Fund money follows students to virtual charters, and the 2025 bills that would have changed it.
Hearing and meeting recordings now have searchable transcripts with timestamps.
Pages that were only pictures of text (scanned slides) are now searchable, so more of each document can be quoted and checked.
Rep. Ricki Ruiz's November 2026 proposals on reserves and a new school cost model.
Upcoming dates for the 2027 session: committee days, the session's start and end, revenue forecasts and the start of the 2027-29 budget period.

The archive's scope now names three questions: how much the state spends, how it's shared (the funding formula) and what it buys (results and accountability). The briefing (since replaced) had new sections on the formula and on results, and four new research issues cover results and accountability.

Online charter schools, filled in: the law changes since 2021, the 2017 state audit of online schools and its follow-up, the split between younger and high school students, and what the largest charters' sponsoring districts say in their own financial records.

The site is reorganized around the decisions being made: a new Start here page, a What's being decided page with the options and who stands where, and new pages on Measures 5 and 50, the Quality Education Model, the funding formula and results. Citations now name their source.
A new Questions page lists what readers have asked, what's answered so far and what's still open, and the menu now groups the reference pages.
Each open question on the Questions page now links to the issue where the research is happening.

What full funding is meant to buy: the Quality Education Commission's model schools and staffing, its assumption that full funding would bring graduation to 90%, the evidence and research it cites, outside critiques, and its fallback options if the full amount isn't funded.
The What's being decided page now explains, in plain words, what a baseline, a benchmark and a proposal are.
The funding chart now appears on the Start here page and next to the State School Fund decision, not only on The numbers.
Three new open questions: whether the Quality Education Model's estimate of need is right, whether corporate kicker money adds to school funding, and whether state mandates on schools are funded.

New page on the Student Investment Account: what the grants may pay for, how much districts spent each year since 2020-21 (mostly on staff, with health and safety the largest category), and how grantees did against their own targets.
SB 1555, the 2026 bill to replace the Quality Education Model, did not pass. The QEM page now explains what it would have done and what a replacement would mean for the funding gap figures.

Confirmed what the November revenue forecast adds for 2027-29: $233.5M more in projected net General Fund revenue, and $244.6M more in available resources counting a larger starting balance. That second figure is the ~$245M in the news.

Gov. Kotek said on Nov 6 that enrollment may be the wrong basis for state school funding and it may have to be student need. Also new: who chaired the education committees in 2026, and the 2027 leadership picks so far, including Rep. Ben Bowman as House Democrats' choice for speaker. Correction: Kotek's September platform doesn't mention enrollment-based funding, as the archive said before; the idea comes from her Nov. 6 remarks.

Who decides now shows each listed legislator's party and district, and the places the Legislature's member page lists for that district. Gov. Tina Kotek's stance against tapping one-time state reserves for PPS, as reported by KATU, is now dated Nov. 6, 2026, not October.

The reader-facing pages now follow one house style: money written out ($12.56 billion, not $12.56B), names spelled out instead of abbreviations like SSF and QEM, and legislators named with their party, district and the places the Legislature lists for it where the archive has their member page. Key terms such as the current service level now have a short, sourced definition where they first appear. No figure changed.
Topic pages now open with our analysis, followed by what the sources say and our calculations. Each analysis names the people, bills and terms it uses, so it reads on its own. No figure changed.

More legislators now carry their party and district on first mention: Speaker Julie Fahey, Rep. Ben Bowman, Sen. Rob Wagner and the sponsors of the 2025 virtual charter bills, with the places the Legislature lists for each district where their member page gives them. Tammy Carpenter is now described as the winner of House District 27 (Beaverton and Cedar Hills) in the unofficial Nov. 3 results, not as a sitting representative.

The State School Fund section of What's being decided now opens with where the decision stands: the archive has no 2027-29 State School Fund amount yet from the Governor or legislative leaders, the Governor's budget is due Dec. 1, and the only proposal in the archive so far is the Portland Public Schools board's request for at least the current service level. No figure changed.

The State School Fund section of What's being decided and the Quality Education Model page now explain what the Quality Education Model's $1.2 billion of state money outside the State School Fund is, how it compares with the $2.2 billion of state grants for K-12 programs, how the current service level is calculated (including pension costs), and what the sources say about what a budget at that level would mean for schools.
The About page now explains how documents are added to the archive and how the analysis is checked before it's published, including that the analysis is written with the help of AI tools.

The online charters page now has the actual pass-through terms for the largest one, Baker Web Academy: for 2025-26 the Baker School District 5J paid it the general legal minimums (80% for K-8 and 95% for grades 9-12 of the state's per-student charter rate), and by our estimate kept about $5.6 million of the General Purpose Grant money for the academy's students. Under the same agreement the district also agreed to provide services such as special education.
The December 2026 revenue forecast, released Nov. 18, 2026, now goes by one name across the site.
The site is now called Oregon Ed Trail, at oregonedtrail.org. The research and links are unchanged.

Every topic page now opens with an "In short": two or three plain sentences on what the page found and what it can't yet say, each backed by the cited evidence below it. Corrected: a news summary had Gov. Tina Kotek opposing one-time reserves for ongoing costs, which the article doesn't say; the reserves page now gives what she said on record.

The overview's key numbers now say what each figure is: the commission's two are its 2027-29 estimates of core state funding, which counts the State School Fund and other state money, and the current service level comes with its definition.

The site has a new design: topic pages open with In short, then our analysis and what the documents say; any linked person, topic, document or abbreviation opens a preview card; and there is search. Every page keeps its address.

What's new now lists new research, data and corrections first, with changes to how the site looks and works in their own section at the end. The overview's latest updates no longer include site changes.

The glossary now explains the four-year graduation rate, the measure the Quality Education Model aims at. Two topic summaries now say their terms in plain words, and the Student Investment Account summary no longer says every district and program sets its own targets.

Pages now list the glossary terms they use in a "Terms on this page" box beside the text, and each glossary term's page lists the pages that use it. The first use of each glossary term on a page links to its definition.

The education department explained its "Charter Schools Rate": it isn't the rate the minimum payments to charter schools are based on. It also said it doesn't publish a dollar total for online schools.

The glossary has one entry for the Legislature's Ways and Means Committee instead of two. Baseline, benchmark and proposal, words this site uses with its own meaning, are no longer linked in the text but still appear under "Terms on this page".

Charts now have their own pages, each with a text version and its sources, all listed under Charts and diagrams. The numbers shows the State School Fund by budget from the same checked files. A new diagram shows how a dollar gets from state taxes and property taxes to a school district. New glossary entries explain local option levies, Lottery Funds, education service districts and high-cost disability grants.
Citations to a meeting recording now name the meeting and open the video at the moment cited, with a link to the archived copy.

What's being decided now has what Gov. Tina Kotek and three Republican legislators said about the December 2026 revenue forecast, set against what the forecast itself says. None named an amount for the State School Fund or mentioned the Education Stability Fund.

What they've said adds State Board of Education Chair Jennifer Scurlock, in May 2026, just before the board adopted rules carrying out Senate Bill 141, the Education Accountability Act: she said she hoped there would be money behind the decisions being made. It is checked against the meeting recording.
